profile.summary: MetageNN assigns long sequencing reads to a genus. It does not align the read against a database: it counts short k-mers, 6-mers in the published setup, and feeds that profile to a neural network. The reason for using short k-mers is that they survive the high error rate of nanopore reads, which lets the model be trained on clean reference genome fragments and still work on noisy reads. Long reads are cut into 1 kbp chunks and the chunk predictions are combined by majority vote.

summary_quotes.text: MetageNN is a neural network model that uses short k-mer profiles of sequences to reduce the impact of distribution shifts on error-prone long reads.
predictions on ONT reads were obtained by segmenting into non-overlapping 1 kbp chunks and using a majority voting strategy (tie broken by highest mean prediction probability)

MetageNN is based on a neural network model that uses short k-mer profiles of sequences to reduce the impact of “distribution shift” when extrapolating from training on genome sequences to testing on error-prone long reads.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Training sequences of fixed length, 1 kbp in the published work, are sampled from reference genomes. Each sequence is turned into a profile of canonical 6-mer counts with the Phylopythia k-mer counting tool, and that vector is the model input: the settings file for the main database gives a k-mer dimension of 6144 and a layer width of 3000, trained for 500 epochs at a learning rate of 0.001 with class weighting and a batch size of 1024. At prediction time a long read is split into non-overlapping 1 kbp chunks, each chunk is classified, and a majority vote decides the read's genus, with ties broken by the highest mean probability and predictions below a probability of 0.5 left unclassified.

sections.title: Databases and training
sections.body: Two reference sets are used. The small database holds 47 genomes, from which about 235,000 sequences of 1 kbp were sampled at 1x coverage for the fine-tuning experiments. The main database expands that about ten times by randomly adding RefSeq representative genomes, giving 516 genomes across 505 species and 311 genera; the model for it was trained at 8x coverage with validation on 200 sequences per genome, and its capacity was roughly doubled in neurons per layer. The paper reports about 17 million samples in that training set, four GPUs and convergence by early stopping after three days.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository is a training setup, not a packaged classifier: it holds one training script, two settings files (small and main database), the genome and isolate lists, and a Google Drive link for the small database 1x training set. No trained weights are published, and the README says the preprint is still to be released, while the published paper exists. What a result must name is the database, the coverage, the k-mer length and the settings file, since those are what differ between the two configurations; the k-mer counting command and the vocabulary dimension have to match each other.

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: A feed forward network over a 6-mer count vector. The main database settings give a k-mer input dimension of 6144 and a layer width of 3000; the paper says the capacity was about doubled in neurons per layer compared with the small database model.

facts.value: A canonical 6-mer count profile per sequence, produced outside the model with the Phylopythia k-mer counting tool. Training sequences were 1 kbp fragments sampled from genomes; long reads are split into non-overlapping 1 kbp chunks.

strengths.text: Short k-mer profiles are the point: they are less affected by sequencing errors, so a model trained on clean genome fragments transfers to noisy long reads without long-read training data.

quotes.text: We use short k-mer-profiles that are known to be less affected by sequencing errors to reduce the “distribution shift” between genome sequences and noisy long reads.

MetageNN overcomes the limitation of not having long-read sequencing-based training data for all organisms by making predictions based on k-mer profiles of sequences collected from a large genome database.

strengths.text: The authors report it as small and fast against the tools they compared: less than a quarter of the database storage of Kraken2, MEGAN-LR and MMseqs2, more than 7 times faster than MetaMaps and GeNet. These are their own figures.

quotes.text: MetageNN requires < 1/4th of the database storage used by Kraken2, MEGAN-LR and MMseqs2 and is > 7× faster than MetaMaps and GeNet

strengths.text: The authors report better sensitivity when the reference database is incomplete, which is the case that matters for novel lineages, and they test it with reads from species deliberately left out of the database.

run_guide.summary: Install the environment, get the small database training set, and train MetageNN on it with the published hyperparameters.
prerequisites: conda. The install script creates a python 3.7 environment with numpy, pandas, pytorch, pytorch-lightning and setuptools 58.2.0.
The small database 1x training dataset, downloaded from the Google Drive link in the repository's data folder, placed where the settings file expects it.
For k-mer counting on your own sequences, the Phylopythia k-mer counting tool (fasta2kmers2) from the repository the README references.
A GPU is expected for a full run: the paper's main database model used four GPUs for three days, although the main database settings file sets gpus to 0.
No licence is declared for the code.

notes: The record's existing source is the MetageNN paper itself, which was fetched in full from PMC (PMC11022314, CC BY 4.0). Two mismatches a reviewer may want to resolve. First, the record's attributes say the main database has 516 RefSeq genomes with a training set of about 17 million 1 kbp sequences at 8x coverage, which the paper supports, while the repository's main database settings file lists total_samples 236212 and a dataset file named training.1x.6mer.npy, that is the 1x small database figures; the sources read do not explain why the main database settings file carries those values. Second, the README says the preprint is to be released, although the paper is published in BMC Bioinformatics; nothing read explains that either. The repository has no licence file and publishes no weights and no prediction script.
